Take this free CAT Probability online test — 10 exam-pattern MCQs with instant scoring and a worked explanation for every answer. The Probability chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Probability tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Probability

Classical probability, the addition rule, independent and mutually exclusive events, and conditional probability.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • P(E) = favourable/total, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
  • P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
  • Independent: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).
  • Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Adding probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events without subtracting the overlap.
  • Confusing independent with mutually exclusive events.
  • Miscounting the sample space.

quiz.title: CAT Probability Practice Quiz
quiz.intro: Ten CAT-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A problem is given to three students A, B, C. P(A solves)=1/2, P(B solves)=1/3, P(C solves)=1/4. All attempt independently. What is the probability the problem is solved?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: P(A doesn't solve) = 1/2, P(B doesn't) = 2/3, P(C doesn't) = 3/4.
Step 2: P(none solves) = (1/2)(2/3)(3/4) = 6/24 = 1/4.
Step 3: P(at least one solves) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.
Answer: 3/4

questions.q: A bag has 4 red and 4 black balls. Four balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 red and 2 black?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Favourable: C(4,2)×C(4,2) = 6×6 = 36.
Step 2: Total: C(8,4) = 70.
Step 3: P = 36/70 = 18/35.
Answer: 18/35

questions.q: Ten cards numbered 1 to 10 are arranged randomly in a row. What is the probability that cards numbered 1 and 2 are adjacent?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Treat cards 1 and 2 as a single block: 9 objects can be arranged in 9! ways.
Step 2: Within the block, 1 and 2 can be arranged in 2! = 2 ways. Favourable = 2 × 9!.
Step 3: Total = 10!. P = 2×9!/10! = 2/10 = 1/5.
Answer: 1/5

questions.q: A game involves rolling two dice. The player wins a amount equal to the sum shown. The entry fee is Rs 7. What is the expected profit per game?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: E(sum of two dice) = E(die1) + E(die2) = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7.
Step 2: Expected winnings = Rs 7. Entry fee = Rs 7.
Step 3: Expected profit = 7 - 7 = Rs 0 (fair game).
Answer: Rs 0

questions.q: Cards are drawn with replacement from a 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a face card on exactly 2 out of 3 draws?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: P(face card) = 12/52 = 3/13. P(not face card) = 10/13.
Step 2: P(exactly 2 face cards) = C(3,2) × (3/13)² × (10/13).
Step 3: = 3 × 9/169 × 10/13 = 270/2197.
Answer: 270/2197

questions.q: A box has 3 red, 5 white, and 2 green balls. Three balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of getting exactly one ball of each colour?
A bag has n red and (n-2) blue balls. The probability of drawing 2 red balls without replacement is 1/3. Find n.
Events A and B have P(A)=x, P(B)=y, P(A ∩ B)=z. Which expression gives P(exactly one of A or B occurs)?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: P(only A) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B) = x - z.
Step 2: P(only B) = P(B) - P(A ∩ B) = y - z.
Step 3: P(exactly one) = (x-z)+(y-z) = x+y-2z.
Answer: x+y-2z

questions.q: Two persons alternate rolling a fair die. The first to roll a 6 wins. Person A rolls first. What is the probability A wins?
A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Three balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that at least 2 are red?

faq.q: Are mutually exclusive and independent the same?
faq.a: No. Mutually exclusive means they can’t both happen (P(A∩B)=0); independent means one doesn’t affect the other (P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)).
P(not E) = 1 − P(E) — often the fastest route for "at least one" questions.
